title: Oliver Stone
wiki_lead:
William Oliver Stone (born September 15, 1946) is an American filmmaker and author. An acclaimed director who tackled subjects ranging from the Vietnam War and American politics to musical biopics and crime dramas, Stone has received numerous accolades including three Academy Awards (plus ten career nominations), a BAFTA Award, a Primetime Emmy, a Satellite Award, a Sant Jordi Award, three Jupiter Awards, three Independent Spirit Awards, and six Golden Globe Awards.
Stone was born in New York City and later briefly attended Yale University. In 1967, Stone enlisted in the United States Army during the Vietnam War. He served from 1967 to 1968 in the 25th Infantry and 1st Cavalry Divisions and was twice wounded in action. For his service, he received military honors including a Bronze Star with "V" Device for valor, Purple Heart with Oak Leaf Cluster (to denote two wounds), an Air Medal and the Combat Infantryman Badge. His service in Vietnam became the foundation for the stark portrayals of war and its aftermath in his work.
Stone began his career as a screenwriter for films such as Midnight Express (1978), for which he won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay, Conan the Barbarian (1982) and Scarface (1983). He then rose to prominence as writer and director of the Vietnam War film dramas Platoon (1986) and Born on the Fourth of July (1989), receiving Academy Awards for Best Director for both films, the former of which also won Best Picture. He also directed Salvador (1986), Wall Street (1987) and its sequel Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps (2010), The Doors (1991), JFK (1991), Heaven & Earth (1993), Natural Born Killers (1994), Nixon (1995), Any Given Sunday (1999), W. (2008) and Snowden (2016). Collectively, his films have grossed $1.3 billion worldwide.
Many of Stone's films focus on controversial American political issues during the late 20th century, and as such were considered contentious at the times of their releases. Stone has been critical of American foreign policy, which he considers to be driven by nationalist and imperialist agendas. Like his subject matter, Stone is a controversial figure in American filmmaking, with some critics accusing him of promoting conspiracy theories.

Early life, education, and military service
William Oliver Stone was born on September 15, 1946, at Doctors Hospital in Yorkville, Manhattan in New York City. He is the only child of Jacqueline (née Goddet) and Louis Stone (born Abraham Louis Silverstein). His parents met in his mother's hometown of Paris during World War II where his father, a U.S. Army colonel, served as a financial officer on General Eisenhower's staff. Upon his return to Manhattan after the war, Louis worked on Wall Street as a stockbroker and investment analyst, eventually becoming vice president of Shearson Lehman Brothers.

grok_lead: William Oliver Stone (born September 15, 1946) is an American filmmaker, screenwriter, and producer whose works frequently explore themes of war, power, and institutional corruption through a lens critical of U.S. government actions. After briefly attending Yale University, Stone enlisted in the U.S. Army in 1967, serving as an infantryman with the 1st Cavalry Division in Vietnam, where he was wounded twiceâonce by shrapnel to the neck and once by a grenadeâand earned the Bronze Star Medal with "V" device for valor, Purple Heart, and other commendations for combat service. He later studied at New York University Film School and broke through as a screenwriter with Midnight Express (1978), for which he won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay; his directorial debut Seizure (1974) was followed by successes like Platoon (1986), a semi-autobiographical Vietnam War film that secured Oscars for Best Picture and Best Director, and Born on the Fourth of July (1989), earning him another Best Director nomination and a Best Adapted Screenplay win. Stone's films such as JFK (1991) and Nixon (1995) have drawn acclaim for stylistic innovation but controversy for advancing unsubstantiated conspiracy theories about historical events, including the Kennedy assassination and Watergate, often prioritizing narrative speculation over empirical evidence. In documentaries like South of the Border (2009), which profiles Latin American leftist leaders, and The Putin Interviews (2017), he has interviewed authoritarian figures sympathetically, critiquing U.S. foreign policy while facing accusations of selective framing that downplays their human rights records and aligns with anti-Western causal narratives unsupported by comprehensive data.
